about: Sourced life stories for the prophets of the New Testament (John the Baptist's story is written elsewhere). Written from Scripture and the reviewed dossier Research/People/prophets-new-testament.md.

simeon-luk-2-25.short: A just and devout man in Jerusalem who took the child Jesus in his arms in the temple and blessed God.

paragraphs.text: Luke introduces Simeon as "a man in Jerusalem", "just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel". The Holy Ghost was upon him, and it had been revealed to him that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ. Luke gives no family, no trade and no age for him.

When Joseph and Mary brought the child Jesus to the temple, to do for him after the custom of the law, Simeon "came by the Spirit into the temple". He took the child up in his arms and blessed God: "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: For mine eyes have seen thy salvation". He spoke of that salvation, prepared "before the face of all people", as "A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel."

Joseph and the child's mother marvelled at what was said. Simeon blessed them and said to Mary that the child was set "for the fall and rising again of many in Israel; and for a sign which shall be spoken against", and that a sword would pierce through her own soul also, "that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed."
At that moment Anna the prophetess came in and gave thanks likewise. Luke says no more of Simeon. He never calls him a prophet, and Scripture does not record his death.

anna-luk-2-36.short: A prophetess of the tribe of Aser, a widow who served God in the temple night and day and spoke of the child Jesus.

paragraphs.text: Luke calls Anna "a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser". She "was of a great age". She had lived with a husband seven years from her virginity, and Luke calls her "a widow of about fourscore and four years".
She "departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day." Scripture does not name her husband.

As Simeon was speaking to Mary in the temple, Anna came in "in that instant". She gave thanks to the Lord, and "spake of him to all them that looked for redemption in Jerusalem." Luke does not record her words, and says no more of her.

agabus-act-11-28.short: A prophet who foretold a great dearth at Antioch; at Caesarea a prophet named Agabus bound himself with Paul's girdle and foretold Paul's binding at Jerusalem.

paragraphs.text: In the days when Barnabas and Saul were teaching at Antioch, prophets came down there from Jerusalem. One of them, Agabus, stood up and "signified by the Spirit that there should be great dearth throughout all the world". Acts adds that it "came to pass in the days of Claudius Cæsar."
The disciples at Antioch, each according to his ability, decided to send relief to the brethren in Judaea, and sent it to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul.

Later in Acts, when Paul's company were staying in the house of Philip the evangelist at Caesarea, "a certain prophet, named Agabus" came down from Judaea; Acts brings him in afresh, without referring back to Antioch. He took Paul's girdle, bound his own hands and feet, and said, "Thus saith the Holy Ghost, So shall the Jews at Jerusalem bind the man that owneth this girdle, and shall deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles."

Paul's companions and the people of the place begged him not to go up to Jerusalem. Paul answered that he was ready "not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus", and they said, "The will of the Lord be done." Acts names Agabus no more.

simeon-act-13-1.short: One of the prophets and teachers in the church at Antioch when the Holy Ghost sent out Barnabas and Saul; Scripture names him once.

paragraphs.text: Acts names "Simeon that was called Niger" second among the "certain prophets and teachers" in the church at Antioch, after Barnabas and before Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen and Saul.

As they ministered to the Lord and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, "Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them." When they had fasted and prayed, they laid their hands on the two and sent them away. Acts does not say which of them the word came through.
Scripture says nothing more of Simeon: not where he came from, nor why he was called Niger, nor what became of him.

lucius-act-13-1.short: Lucius of Cyrene, one of the prophets and teachers at Antioch when Barnabas and Saul were sent out.

paragraphs.text: Acts names "Lucius of Cyrene" among the "certain prophets and teachers" in the church at Antioch, with Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Manaen and Saul. Earlier, Acts tells that men of Cyprus and Cyrene had come to Antioch and spoken to the Grecians, "preaching the Lord Jesus"; it does not name them.

As they ministered to the Lord and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, "Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them." After fasting and prayer they laid their hands on the two and sent them away.

In his letter to the Romans, Paul sends greetings from "Lucius, and Jason, and Sosipater, my kinsmen". Scripture does not say whether this is the same Lucius, and says nothing more of Lucius of Cyrene.

manaen-act-13-1.short: A man brought up with Herod the tetrarch, named among the prophets and teachers at Antioch.

paragraphs.text: Acts names Manaen among the "certain prophets and teachers" in the church at Antioch, and says he "had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch". In Luke's Gospel "Herod the tetrarch" is the Herod who was tetrarch of Galilee, who had John the Baptist beheaded.

As the prophets and teachers ministered to the Lord and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, "Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them." They fasted and prayed, laid their hands on the two, and sent them away.
Scripture says nothing more of Manaen: not how he came to believe, nor what became of him.

bar-jesus-act-13-6.short: A Jewish sorcerer at Paphos whom Acts calls "a false prophet"; he withstood Barnabas and Saul and was struck blind for a season.

paragraphs.text: When Barnabas and Saul had gone through the isle of Cyprus to Paphos, they found "a certain sorcerer, a false prophet, a Jew, whose name was Bar-jesus". He was with the deputy of the country, Sergius Paulus, "a prudent man", who called for Barnabas and Saul and wanted to hear the word of God.
Acts also calls him "Elymas the sorcerer (for so is his name by interpretation)". He withstood them, "seeking to turn away the deputy from the faith." Acts records no word of his.

Saul, "filled with the Holy Ghost", set his eyes on him and called him "thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness". He told him, "thou shalt be blind, not seeing the sun for a season." At once a mist and a darkness fell on him, and he went about seeking someone to lead him by the hand.
When the deputy saw what was done, he believed, "being astonished at the doctrine of the Lord." Acts does not say whether Bar-jesus saw again, or what became of him.

judas-act-15-22.short: Judas surnamed Barsabas, a prophet and one of the chief men at Jerusalem, sent with Silas to carry the apostles' letter to Antioch.

paragraphs.text: After the apostles and elders had come together at Jerusalem, they, with the whole church, chose "Judas surnamed Barsabas, and Silas, chief men among the brethren" to go to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They carried a letter, which said that Judas and Silas would "also tell you the same things by mouth."

At Antioch they gathered the multitude and delivered the letter, and the people "rejoiced for the consolation." Judas and Silas, "being prophets also themselves, exhorted the brethren with many words, and confirmed them." Acts does not record what they said.

After a time they were let go in peace from the brethren to the apostles. Acts names Judas no more. The only other person Scripture calls Barsabas is Joseph called Barsabas, put forward with Matthias in Acts 1; Scripture does not say whether the two were related.
